quote: What do you want me to do for you?
firstReading: Revelation opens by identifying its message as an unveiling given by God through Jesus Christ for the servants who must heed what is soon to occur. John greets the churches with grace and peace, then addresses Ephesus. The risen Christ knows its labor, endurance, doctrinal vigilance, and rejection of false apostles. Yet he reproves the community for abandoning its first love, calling it to remember, repent, and return to its former works.
psalmSummary: Psalm 1 contrasts the way of the righteous with the way of the wicked. Blessed people refuse the counsel and path of sinners, finding their delight instead in the law of the Lord and meditating upon it continually. They are like a fruitful tree planted beside running water, secure and life-giving. The wicked, however, are unstable and cannot stand in judgment, for the Lord watches over the righteous way.
gospelSummary: As Jesus approaches Jericho, a blind man sitting beside the road hears that Jesus is passing and cries out to him as the Son of David. Those around him try to silence him, but he calls out all the more insistently for mercy. Jesus stops, has the man brought near, and asks what he desires. The man asks to receive his sight. Jesus declares that his faith has saved him, and he immediately sees. The healed man follows Jesus, glorifying God, while the people who witness the miracle give praise to God.
saintReflection: Saint Margaret of Scotland (Optional Memorial): Saint Margaret of Scotland (c. 1045–1093) became queen through marriage to King Malcolm III and sought to order royal life toward worship, justice, and care for the poor. She supported the reform of ecclesial practices, encouraged education and prayer, founded churches and works of mercy, and personally served people in need. Her marriage and family life were shaped by the conviction that public responsibility remains accountable to the law of Christ. Margaret's holiness did not arise from rank but from grace received through prayer, the sacraments, and charity. On a day that also remembers Saint Gertrude, the Church is invited to join active mercy with contemplation. Margaret calls believers to reverence in worship, generosity toward the poor, responsible family life, and authority exercised as humble service before God.
dailyPrayer:
Lord Jesus Christ, Son of David, turn toward us in mercy as you turned toward the blind man near Jericho. Heal the blindness that keeps us from recognizing your presence, receiving your word, and loving you with an undivided heart. Grant us the grace to remember the love to which you first called us, to repent of our coldness, and to return to the works of charity that flow from communion with you.

Through the intercession of Saint Margaret of Scotland, form our homes, parishes, and communities in reverence for worship, fidelity to the sacraments, generosity toward the poor, and humble service. Teach those entrusted with authority to remain obedient to your law and attentive to those in need. May prayer bear fruit in merciful action, and may mercy lead us more deeply into prayer. Let us follow you with thankful hearts and join all creation in giving glory to God. Amen.
theologicalSynthesis:
The readings reveal that Christian perseverance is not merely the endurance of hardship or the defense of true teaching. Christ praises the Church at Ephesus for its labor and discernment, yet calls it back to its first love. The law of the Lord, celebrated in Psalm 1, is not an external burden but the life-giving way by which the faithful are rooted in God. In the Gospel, the blind man embodies this return: he refuses every attempt to silence his plea, recognizes Jesus as the promised Son of David, and receives sight through faith.

Saint Margaret of Scotland witnesses to this ordered love in worship, mercy, family life, and public responsibility. Her service of the poor and care for ecclesial life were to arise from grace, prayer, and sacramental communion. The Church therefore asks not only for clear vision but for a heart renewed in love, so that faith may glorify God through concrete charity.
exegesis:
Context: The opening of Revelation identifies the book as an unveiling whose ultimate source is God and whose center is Jesus Christ. Its purpose is not to satisfy curiosity about hidden events but to summon Christ’s servants to faithful hearing and obedience. John writes to concrete churches, communities living amid pressures that test worship, doctrine, endurance, and moral fidelity. The greeting of grace and peace establishes that the Church’s life begins in God’s gift before it becomes a task. Revelation speaks with urgency because the Lord’s coming gives present conduct its serious weight.

Context: The message to Ephesus shows the searching knowledge of the risen Christ. He knows the community’s works, toil, patient endurance, and refusal to accept false claimants to apostolic authority. These are genuine goods; truth matters, and the Church must discern teaching that contradicts the apostolic faith. Yet Christ’s judgment reaches deeper than outward fidelity. The community has left its first love. This is not a dismissal of doctrinal vigilance or persevering labor, but a warning that neither can replace loving communion with the Lord. The command to remember, repent, and do the former works presents conversion as a return to the source from which authentic ecclesial action flows. The warning concerning the lampstand underscores that a church’s visible witness cannot endure when love for Christ has grown cold.

Psalm: Psalm 1 provides the wisdom framework for this call. The blessed person does not shape life by the counsel, path, or settled company of sin, but delights in the law of the Lord. Biblical law here is not opposed to grace. It is the graciously revealed way that forms a people in covenant communion with God. Meditation upon that law means sustained receptivity, allowing God’s will to judge and direct desire. The image of the tree by flowing water portrays stability and fruitfulness received from a living source. This illumines the Ephesian exhortation: works become fruitful when they are nourished by love for God. Conversely, the wicked are compared to chaff, not because divine judgment is arbitrary, but because a life detached from God lacks enduring substance. The Lord knows the way of the righteous, a knowledge of covenantal care and judgment.

Gospel: Luke places the healing near Jericho as Jesus continues toward Jerusalem, where his messianic mission will reach its paschal fulfillment. The blind man cannot see Jesus physically, yet he perceives his identity more clearly than those who would silence him. His invocation of Jesus as Son of David confesses messianic hope: the one passing by is the promised king who brings God’s saving mercy. His persistence is integral to the scene. Crowds attempt to restrain his cry, but need and faith make him call out more earnestly. Jesus stops. The Lord who journeys toward suffering is not inaccessible to the plea of one in darkness.

Gospel: Jesus’ question does not arise from ignorance; it draws the man into a personal expression of faith and desire. The request for sight is answered with a declaration that his faith has saved him. Physical healing is immediate, but Luke presents more than restored vision. The man follows Jesus and glorifies God, indicating discipleship and worship. The crowd also gives praise to God, so mercy becomes public doxology. The episode teaches that salvation brings a person from the roadside into the way of following Christ. It also reveals the proper response to grace: not silent possession of a gift, but praise of God and a life ordered after Jesus. The Gospel thereby answers the concern raised in Revelation. First love is renewed where believers cry to Christ, receive his mercy, and follow him in worshipful gratitude.

Saints: Saint Margaret of Scotland offers a fitting witness to this scriptural pattern. Her life, as presented by the Church, joined reverence in worship, concern for ecclesial reform, education, prayer, and concrete mercy toward people in need. Her royal station did not constitute holiness; grace received in prayer, the sacraments, and charity did. In light of Revelation, her example recalls that responsibility within family and public life remains accountable to the law of Christ. In light of Psalm 1, her works of mercy and support for the Church may be understood as fruit borne by a life seeking delight in God’s will. Her personal service of those in need also reflects the Gospel’s refusal to let the vulnerable remain unseen or unheard. The remembrance of Saint Gertrude alongside Margaret further invites the Church to hold contemplation and active mercy together, without separating devotion from love of neighbor.

Today: The readings call the faithful to examine whether perseverance has remained living and loving. It is possible to retain sound words, sustain many labors, and yet need to return to the heart of discipleship: love of Christ that becomes love of his members. The blind man teaches holy insistence in prayer. Those conscious of darkness are not to be discouraged by obstacles, by public disapproval, or by their own weakness; they are to cry to the merciful Lord. Psalm 1 directs this prayer toward habitual meditation on God’s law, so that the believer may be rooted rather than scattered. Saint Margaret directs the same conversion toward worship, family life, care for the poor, and humble service. Christ grants sight not for self-enclosure, but so that his disciples may follow him and glorify God.
